questions.q: What is an access certification campaign?
options: An automated script that silently removes all dormant accounts every night
A marketing campaign used to promote a new identity governance tool
A periodic, structured review where managers or resource owners must explicitly decide to keep or revoke each access grant
A one-time audit performed only when a new employee is hired
questions.explain: Certification campaigns are a deliberate, scheduled human review, not an automated scan — the whole point is getting someone with real context to make an explicit decision.

questions.q: Why is the user's manager or the resource/application owner the one who certifies access, rather than IT alone?
options: IT can see that someone has access, but only the manager or owner can credibly say whether they still need it
Resource owners have no knowledge of their own systems, so IT must decide instead
IT staff are not legally permitted to view access lists
Managers are required by law to approve all access requests
questions.explain: Certifying access requires business context about whether a grant is still needed for someone's current role — context IT alone doesn't have.

questions.q: Why do most organizations run access certification campaigns on a quarterly or semi-annual schedule instead of continuously?
options: Running reviews more often than once a year is against industry regulation
A scheduled campaign with a deadline creates real accountability, while a constant trickle of micro-reviews gets ignored more easily
Quarterly reviews are required by every company's IT department regardless of risk level
Continuous review is technically impossible in any identity system
questions.explain: A defined campaign with a hard deadline and tracked completion gets attention that an unscheduled, continuous process typically doesn't.

questions.q: What happens to an access grant that is not explicitly attested to by the campaign deadline?
options: It is revoked automatically — the absence of a decision is treated as a 'no,' not a 'yes'
It is automatically kept, since no objection was raised
It is escalated to the CEO for a final decision
Nothing happens until the next campaign a year later
questions.explain: Attestation defaults to revocation, not approval — this is what prevents reviewers from rubber-stamping an entire list without reading it.

questions.q: In the lesson's example, why did David's vendor payment approval access get flagged during the quarterly campaign?
options: His current manager could not confidently confirm he still needed it, since it was left over from an earlier stint on the AP team
David requested that his own access be revoked
David had been terminated the week before the campaign ran
The ERP system automatically flags all vendor-related permissions every quarter
questions.explain: The campaign surfaced access that had quietly survived a role change — exactly the mover-driven access creep described in Lesson 21.
